Ask HN: I have been unemployed for 2y. 15 years of experience, US. What to do?
stories.text:
I'm Senior software engineer in the US (DMV area), with 15y of experience. Worked for Fortune 50+ company and bunch of mid-size companies. Been unemployed for 2y and can't find a job, within those 2 years, I pretty much spent my savings that I've saved through years, maybe have 4-5 months left to support my household. Currently, I tutor math and probably about to start working as manager in pizzaria.

In Jan 2025, I quit from a mid-size insurance tech company(1000+) after working there for almost 4y, because I was tipped off the they were about to start layoffs and they did. Well, since then I have zero luck finding any job in SWE.

At this point, I have massive gap in my resume that I can't explain to recruiters, I can still code (C#/.NET/AWS) and learned the AI, but who cares if date of my last employment is Jan2025. What should I do ?

If you have an alternative path (something completely different from SWE or SWE adjacent) that pays "well", I would like to hear.

Show HN: OpenComputer – an open source alternative to Devin
stories.text:
Hi HN!

Utpal here, I'm one of the founders of OpenComputer.

OpenComputer is an open source cloud coding agent for teams that can run in your own cloud account (AWS, GCP, Azure).

We run the agent harness and the sandbox on the same durable VM (architecture in the docs [1]). First commit lands in 24s; the alternatives we benchmarked took 53-72s (benchmarks below [2]).

Two other choices:

- One VM per team, scalable horizontally. Sessions are isolated in git worktrees. - Session files are backed up to a repo after every turn, so any session can resume on another VM.

We noticed that past ~640 session-hours a month, one always-on 4 vCPU VM is cheaper than per-session E2B sandboxes, for example. So at scale, this setup would not only be faster than current SOTA coding agents, but also more cost-efficient.

Feel free to try via cloud for free [4] or self host. We would love any and all feedback, and happy to answer any questions! Full demo below [3].

[1]: https://docs.opencomputer.dev/getting-started/architecture [2]: https://opencomputer.dev/blog/cloud-agents-as-fast-as-local/ [3]: https://x.com/IgorZIJ/status/2121309785882591711 [4]: https://app.opencomputer.dev

Tell HN: OpenRouter prompts to Minimax may have been read
stories.text:
I received the following email from OpenRouter and it appears authentic. There is no public page or blog post.

--

Title: Requests you sent to MiniMax models may have been read

Hi there,

A security researcher placed unique test URLs in prompts sent to MiniMax models from July to October 2026. A third party accessed those URLs 40 to 130 hours after the requests were sent, whether MiniMax served a request directly or another provider forwarded it to MiniMax. With one exception, the same tests on other models at those providers were not accessed, and none of the AWS test keys were used.

Your account sent [redacted] requests to MiniMax models through MiniMax and Novita, from [redacted] to [redacted] UTC.

AtlasCloud, Novita and StreamLake have told us they forwarded OpenRouter requests for MiniMax models to MiniMax. Based on what the researcher and these providers have reported, the issue sits with MiniMax and the providers that forwarded to it, not with OpenRouter. We are passing on what they have told us. MiniMax told StreamLake that content moderation was enabled on its endpoints before October 22 and that it has since enabled Zero Data Retention. We have asked MiniMax for its own account and have not received one.

This means a third party may have read the prompts and outputs of these requests. While we investigate, we have removed the Zero Data Retention label from these MiniMax-model endpoints.

stories.title: Ask HN: Should Uber Ratings Decay over Time?
stories.text:
I’ve been thinking about how platforms like Uber calculate reputation scores, and I believe there’s a fundamental flaw in how historical ratings are treated.

Uber calculates passenger ratings using the last 500 rated trips, regardless of when those trips occurred.

In my case, I have 455 ratings, 426 of which are five stars (93.6%). My overall rating is 4.86.

What bothers me isn’t the score itself, but the underlying methodology.

A negative rating from five years ago can carry exactly the same weight as one received yesterday. And if you’re an infrequent user who hasn’t accumulated 500 ratings, that negative feedback could influence your reputation for years.

This raises an interesting question: Should reputation systems measure your historical average, or should they attempt to represent who you are today?

One possible solution is exponential time decay:

Weight = 2^(-t/H)

Where t is the age of the rating and H is a half-life, perhaps 12 months.

Under that approach, a rating from one year ago would carry 50% of its original weight, and one from two years ago just 25%.

Of course, this introduces other challenges. How do you prevent someone with a history of poor behaviour from simply waiting for their reputation to recover? How do you maintain statistical confidence for infrequent users? Would Bayesian smoothing or a minimum effective sample size help?

There’s also a broader philosophical question around the right to be forgotten. Should digital reputation systems indefinitely preserve the consequences of historical assessments, particularly when those assessments are subjective and potentially no longer representative?

I’m curious how others would approach this.

* Is a rolling window of 500 ratings statistically defensible without considering time? * Would exponential decay produce a fairer and more predictive reputation score? * Should platforms expose both a lifetime rating and a recent-behaviour rating? * Are there better approaches already being used in other reputation systems?

I’d be particularly interested in perspectives from people who’ve worked on marketplace ranking, trust and safety, or reputation algorithms.

It seems like a relatively simple mathematical change, but one with potentially significant implications for fairness across digital platforms.

This Industrial Revolution Belongs to the Builders
stories.text:
You've heard AI = Labor. Therefore Labor -> 0.

Some people think this means that only asset owners, people with lots of capital, will come out ahead.

They're wrong.

Because as a builder/founder, you create value.

Capital must capture some of this value to have a return.

The reason founders primarily need capital is to pay for labor (either employees or supplier overhead).

So this means that Capital ~= Labor.

But that's a problem for the "owners of capital will own everything" narrative, because now we have:

AI = Labor = Capital -> 0

In practice this will happen slowly as builders need less and less capital to build, capital will increasingly struggle to capture value created by builders.

Counterintuitively this means valuations will climb dramatically reflecting capital paying more and more to capture less and less value from builders.

As disruption accelerates, volatility increases while broader market wide returns start to stagnate.

The net will be a wholesale wealth and power transfer from capital holders to builders/founders, on the magnitude of what happened between the aristocracy and the capitalist class in the earlier industrial revolutions.

It's already started, companies are raising later and at higher valuations.

Most people accept that if superintelligence were created, capital would be useless, but what they often don't realize is that a class of builders armed with AI is already creating a distributed superintelligence that will have the same effect.

Interested if anyone else shares this perspective.

Ask HN: What's stopping us from putting agents in general purpose robots?
stories.text:
After using Claude a bunch in the last few months I can't stop thinking the obvious next logical step is to put an agent in a physical robot

For example imagine asking "can you go into the other room, find object X, and bring it to me"

It seems to me the intelligence/reasoning ability is more than enough for something like that

And giving models images they seem to be able to recognize objects well to understand what they are looking at

But its not clear to me what is holding this product area back.

Is it a matter of the speed of the update loop or number of iterations it takes the agent being too slow to be practical?

Or does interpreting images/video cause the context/cost to blow up?
